question: A 70-year-old man with known ischaemic heart disease (previous STEMI 2 years ago) presents with melaena. His haemoglobin is 8.5 g/dL and he is haemodynamically stable. He is not actively bleeding. What is the most appropriate transfusion decision?

answers.text: Transfuse immediately — haemoglobin <10 g/dL always requires transfusion in the elderly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no evidence-based threshold of Hb <10 g/dL for universal transfusion. Liberal transfusion at this level is associated with higher re-bleeding rates, portal pressure increases in cirrhosis, and no mortality benefit. Age alone is not an indication for liberal transfusion.

answers.text: Do not transfuse — maintain the standard restrictive threshold of Hb <7 g/dL regardless of cardiac history

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The standard restrictive threshold of Hb <7 g/dL applies to patients WITHOUT cardiovascular disease. In patients with ischaemic heart disease or cardiac failure, the threshold is raised to Hb <8 g/dL to protect against myocardial ischaemia triggered by anaemia.

answers.text: Transfuse — this patient meets the modified threshold of Hb <8 g/dL applicable in ischaemic heart disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In patients with ischaemic heart disease (or other significant cardiovascular disease), the restrictive transfusion threshold is raised to Hb <8 g/dL. At 8.5 g/dL the patient is at threshold. However since he is at 8.5 and the threshold is <8, technically he does not yet meet the trigger — the precise threshold matters. In clinical practice with active GI bleeding history and IHD, transfusion at 8.5 approaching 8 is appropriate to prevent the threshold being crossed during ongoing slow loss.

answers.text: Await repeat haemoglobin in 6 hours before deciding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While serial haemoglobin monitoring is appropriate, a haemodynamically stable patient with IHD and Hb approaching the 8 g/dL modified threshold in the context of active GI bleeding should have a proactive transfusion plan rather than waiting for deterioration.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the transfusion section. The standard restrictive threshold is Hb <7 g/dL; this is modified to <8 g/dL in ischaemic heart disease or cardiac failure. Liberal transfusion (>10 g/dL) worsens outcomes in GI bleeding — it raises portal pressure in varices and is associated with higher re-bleeding rates.

The key learning point: restrictive threshold is Hb <7 g/dL for most patients, but raised to <8 g/dL in cardiovascular disease (IHD, cardiac failure). This modification is explicitly evidence-based and reflects the higher myocardial oxygen demand in coronary artery disease.
